narrative:
The model estimated a 93% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is a high-risk estimate, not a certainty, but it is the reason your law school application was denied: the decision treated predicted bar-exam failure as a serious academic-risk signal.

The strongest factor was your third-year class standing. You were in the second decile, compared with an average around the sixth decile among accepted students, and this pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. The next most influential factor was your LSAT score of 28, well below the accepted-student average of about 37, which also pushed toward failure. Your first-year class standing was the third most important factor; again, a second-decile position versus an accepted average near the sixth decile added to the failure risk. These academic indicators outweighed your undergraduate GPA of 3.60, which was above the accepted average, because they were more influential in the model’s risk estimate.

To improve your position, focus on factors you can still change: prepare for and retake the LSAT, seek admissions counseling about how to address your class standing, and consider strengthening your record through additional legal or graduate coursework before reapplying. Ask the admissions office for feedback and apply to a balanced range of programs.
